name: Ile de la Cite
short_description: Heart of ancient Paris and one of two natural Seine islands, where the Parisii tribe first settled and Notre-Dame was built

beats.script_body: The Ile de la Cite was the first part of Paris to be settled, occupied by the Celtic tribe of the Parisii in the 3rd century BC, making it the original nucleus of the city. In the 3rd century AD, the Roman Emperor Julian established his seat on the island, on the site of today's Palais de Justice — it was here in 360 that he was proclaimed emperor by his own soldiers. In the 6th century, the Merovingian king Childebert made it the permanent home of the kings of France. And in the 13th century, the pious Louis IX built a private chapel adjoining the palace — la Chapelle Royale, now known as la Sainte-Chapelle — to house a piece of the Holy Cross and the Crown of Thorns he had bought from the last Emperor of Constantinople.
beats.source_passage: the Celtic tribe of the Parisi, the early inhabitants of Paris who in the 3rd century BC occupied I'Ile de la Cite

opening_hours_basis: An open Seine island of streets, quays and squares whose value stands in the open, not behind any gate.
visit_basis: Whole Seine island of quays, squares and lanes to walk across between Notre-Dame and Pont Neuf; a setting explored on foot with no single interior to enter here.
judgement_basis: This island is threaded by trafficked streets with quays dropping to the river so a child at speed is unsafe, but it has open squares and benches (place Dauphine, cathedral forecourt) quiet enough to sit and talk, and it stays lit, central and peopled after dark.
queue_basis: This is an open island of streets, bridges, and squares with no gated interior, so there is no line to enter it.

name: Jardin des Tuileries
short_description: Former royal garden designed by Andre Le Notre where Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette were held under house arrest after the Bastille fell

beats.script_body: On 6 October 1789, roughly a century after Louis XIV had moved the court to Versailles, the infuriated people of Paris transferred his great-great-grandson Louis XVI back. The days of absolutism were over and it was now the King's turn to be kept in check. Heading from Versailles to the Tuileries — the Louvre being too dilapidated to inhabit — the royal coach was made to follow a long and strange procession of National Guards, royal troops, excited throngs of Parisians, and carts of corn and flour escorted by sharp-eyed mutinous women. The Tuileries then replaced the Louvre as the residence of every subsequent king and emperor of France.
beats.source_passage: the royal coach was made to follow a long and strange procession of National Guards, royal troops, excited throngs of Parisians and carts of corn and flour

beats.script_body: The Palais des Tuileries, built by Catherine de Medici in 1564, served as the seat of French power through every regime change of the 19th century. After his coup on 2 December 1851, Louis Napoleon promptly left the Republican Palais de l'Elysee for the royal Tuileries — the last ruler to use it. When the nascent Third Republic came to power after defeating the Paris Commune in 1871, it moved out of the 1st arrondissement entirely, heading west to the Palais de l'Elysee — the home of the Republic's Presidents ever since. The fire that had damaged the Tuileries during the Commune had tolled the knell of the arrondissement as the seat of power. In 1882, rather than restore the charred carcass, the Third Republic razed the Tuileries to the ground, 'securing irrevocably the definitive death of the monarchy.'
beats.source_passage: rather than restore the charred carcass of the Palais des Tuileries, the Third Republic razed it to the ground, securing irrevocably the definitive death of the monarchy

opening_hours_basis: Gated garden with closing gates; transcribed from OSM tag 'Mo-Su 07:30-21:00'.
visit_basis: Large formal royal garden with long gravel allees, fountains, statues and terraces between the Louvre and Concorde; walking its length and pausing at the basins fills the better part of an hour, open-air throughout.
judgement_basis: A large enclosed traffic-free royal garden with gravel paths, lawns and abundant free movable chairs and benches where children can run and two people can talk quietly, but the garden is gated and closed at night.
queue_basis: A public royal garden entered through open gateways from the street with no ticket or screening, so visitors walk straight in.

anchors.label: The central pool
anchors.basis: The garden's round basin — the corpus's own Grand Bassin Rond record pins it — is where a person stands at the pool the Supreme Being ceremony departed from, nearly three hundred metres from the garden pin.

anchors.label: The Jardin du Carrousel
anchors.basis: The Carrousel garden fills the eastern end between the Arc du Carrousel and the Tuileries proper; a person stands on its lawns under the arch's sightline, four hundred metres east of the mid-garden pin.

anchors.label: The octagonal basin
anchors.basis: The Grand Bassin Octogonal fills the western end just inside the Place de la Concorde gates; a person stands at its rim with Le Silence and the basin's edge in front of them, nearly four hundred metres west of the garden pin.

name: Les Halles
short_description: Site of Paris's central food market for 800 years from 1135 until its controversial demolition in 1969, now the Forum des Halles shopping centre

beats.script_body: The central market of Les Halles was Paris's pulsating lifeblood for nearly eight hundred years. In 1135, Louis VI set up a primitive market on land allotted by the Bishop of Paris, against a return of a third of its revenue. The marshy fields around it gave it its first name — Les Champeaux. In 1183, Philippe-Auguste replaced the open market with two stone buildings to shelter goods and vendors in bad weather, securing them with locks to prevent thefts. To raise the funds for the project, he confiscated the possessions of the Jews. The market became known as Les Halles — 'pour ce que chacun y allait,' for everyone went there — and the name stuck for eight centuries.
beats.source_passage: In 1135 Louis VI set up a primitive market on a piece of land allotted by the Bishop of Paris

beats.script_body: By the mid-19th century, France had entered the Industrial Age and iron was replacing stone. Impressed by Victor Baltard's newly built Gare de l'Est, Napoleon III commissioned him to rebuild the Les Halles market with a memorable instruction: 'Faites-moi des parapluies!' — make me umbrellas. Fourteen iron pavilions rose between 1851 and 1857, an artistic expression of the Industrial Revolution that stood for over a century. In 1969, the market was controversially transferred to Rungis south of Paris and the pavilions demolished. Only one of the fourteen survived, moved to the suburb of Nogent-sur-Marne. Sculptor Raymond Mason mourned: 'It was a place of bliss... the last vision of natural life in the City. It is now Paradise lost.' Social observer Louis Chevalier was blunter: 'The death of Les Halles has tolled the knell of Paris.'
beats.source_passage: Napoleon III commissioned him to build the new market, commending the use of iron: Faites-moi des parapluies!

beats.script_body: Emile Zola dubbed Les Halles 'the belly of Paris,' a metaphor he used in 1873 for the title of one of his novels. For a year he haunted the market at all hours, recording the ever-changing hues of this gigantic digestive apparatus of the capital: dark bluish-grey metal structures against a light grey sky in wet weather, sheets of gold as the sun's rays penetrate on a fine day, glowing glass panes at sunset. He watched the robust porters — les forts des Halles, 'all nerves and muscles' — and descended into the undisclosable underground depths where the slaughter of fowl was carried out nightly, a place reeking of blood and pestilence and overrun by rats. This underworld was unknown to the bourgeois and the artist who, after a night at a cabaret, would drift to the market for onion soup and strong emotions.
beats.source_passage: Emile Zola had dubbed its plebeian eastern parts 'the belly of Paris' a metaphor he used in 1873 for the title of one of his novels

beats.script_body: The Dames des Halles — the market's notorious fishwives — occupied a unique position in Parisian society. On special occasions they were allowed into the King's Palace to pay their respects to the royal couple, and after a hearty meal they would return to Les Halles to pass on the latest Palace gossip. On 30 August 1608, one Femme Ladoucette wrote an astonishing letter to Marie de Medici, Henri IV's second wife. Having introduced herself as Dame des Halles 'from mother to daughter since Saint Louis,' she proceeded to complain about the King's philandering: a good fellow deep down, she wrote, but who 'fidgets at the sight of a coquette and scatters bastards around, although blessed with a most appetising Queen, so well conditioned to have little princes.' If the King wandered through Les Halles, she threatened, she would give him a sound thrashing for the love of her Queen. Femme Ladoucette received no scolding — instead she was promoted 'fournisseuse royale.'
beats.source_passage: Femme Ladoucette received no scolding for her bold letter - instead she was promoted fournisseuse royale

beats.script_body: With its ceaseless human tide, Les Halles was picked out for public executions and punishments from the 14th century onward. Decapitations were preceded by customary torture and followed by the mutilation of bodies. The King's pillory, the largest of them all, was a sizeable octagonal structure with a pointed roof and weathervane, somewhat resembling a chapel. The ground floor was often inhabited by the King's Great Executioner, while the convicts were exposed in the tower above. The excited mob relished the spectacle, taunting exposed victims and pelting them with rubbish and litter. There were no gallows, however — the King conceding that the market was no place for bodies to be left rotting on a rope.
beats.source_passage: the King's pillory, the largest of them all, was a sizeable octagonal structure, with a pointed roof and weathervane, somewhat resembling a chapel

opening_hours_basis: Named as a historic market site and present-day district setting rather than an entered venue, so treated as an open urban setting and not gated.
visit_basis: Site of the former market, now the Forum des Halles with its Canopy roof and surrounding gardens; the mall interior and levels absorb around 40 min if entered.
judgement_basis: A large shopping-centre-and-garden complex where children cannot run free among crowds and roads, but the surrounding Nelson Mandela garden has free benches and lawns quiet enough to talk, and the area is lit and busy well into the night.
queue_basis: The Forum des Halles is an open shopping centre with multiple free entrances and no admission control, so nobody waits to enter.

name: Louvre Museum
short_description: World's largest art museum with 35,000 works on display, housed in a former royal fortress transformed into a palace

beats.script_body: The Louvre began not as a museum but as a military fortress. In 1190, Philippe-Auguste built it as a defence tower before embarking on the Third Crusade, wary that the English might invade via the Seine — the same route the Norsemen had used three centuries earlier to devastate Paris. He placed it at the westernmost point of the right bank fortification, facing the Tour de Nesle across the river, with the Plantagenets not far downstream at Gisors in Normandy. A wall 3,000 metres long, 3 metres thick and 10 metres high encircled the right bank, and upon his return in 1191, Philippe-Auguste deposited the Crown treasures and archives inside the Louvre, considering it the safest place in the capital. The fortress became known as 'la plus halte tor de Paris la citet' — the tallest tower in Paris the city.
beats.source_passage: he erected the Louvre on the right bank, at the westernmost point of the fortification, facing the Tour de Nesle on the opposite bank

beats.script_body: Charles V began transforming the Louvre into his residence when he became king in 1364. In 1368, he repurposed the northwest tower — formerly known as the Tour de la Fauconnerie — into the first royal library of France, housing over nine hundred manuscripts. This collection was the seed of what would eventually become the Bibliotheque Nationale.
beats.source_passage: he collected within its thick walls the kingdom's manuscripts and founded the first royal library of France

beats.script_body: In 1528, Francois I demolished the medieval Louvre fortress to build a Renaissance palace, and Parisians were genuinely upset. They mourned the loss of 'la Grosse Tour,' the great tower where Charles V used to read and meditate. But Francois had personal reasons for hating fortresses: he had just been released from the fortress of Madrid, where Emperor Charles V of Spain had kept him captive after defeating him at the Battle of Pavia in 1525. His rebuilt Louvre became a backdrop for extravagant celebrations designed to humiliate his former captor. When the Emperor visited in 1540, every weather vane had been gilded, the window panes coloured, and the staircases illuminated with brass candlesticks — all to dazzle and humble the man who had once imprisoned him.
beats.source_passage: The people of Paris were quite upset by the sudden disappearance in 1528 of 'la Grosse Tour', where Charles V used to read and meditate

beats.script_body: Francois I didn't just rebuild the Louvre — he gave it its artistic soul. He bestowed the spirit of the Renaissance upon the palace and started the painting collection that would one day make it the largest painting museum in the world. His was an embryonic collection, but it already comprised works by Leonardo da Vinci, Raphael, and Titian. Most notably, Leonardo himself brought the Mona Lisa to France when he accepted Francois I's invitation in 1516, spending his final years at the Chateau d'Amboise under royal patronage. After Leonardo's death on 2 May 1519, his assistant Salai inherited the painting and sold it to the King for 4,000 gold coins.
beats.source_passage: the most renowned painting in the Louvre, the Mona Lisa, which Francois I is believed to have transferred to Paris from Amboise after the death of da Vinci in 1519

beats.script_body: Henri IV entered Paris on 22 March 1594, four years after his accession, having converted to Catholicism with the famous words 'Paris vaut bien une messe' — Paris is well worth a mass. His architectural ambition was immediate: he set out to connect the Louvre to the Palais des Tuileries via a colossal 460-metre wing along the Seine called La Grande Galerie, also known as la Galerie du Bord de l'Eau. A Swiss visitor confirmed the scale when he wrote that 'the edifice is so pompous and so vast that once completed there will be no other like it in all Christendom.' The gallery was completed by the elegant Pavillon de Flore at its western end, but the gigantic enterprise was a constant headache for his minister Sully, who had to squeeze segments of the population dry to raise funds.
beats.source_passage: a colossal wing of monumental grandeur - 470 metres long - La Grande Galerie, also known as la Galerie du Bord de l'Eau

beats.script_body: Henri IV's Grande Galerie wasn't built for display — it was built to house the best artisans and artists of the kingdom, realizing an artistic mission he had set for the Louvre. The palace became the home of both royalty, with their 1,500-strong army of servants, and a select artistic community living alongside them. This intimate coexistence of high and low was a hallmark of the 1st arrondissement that persisted for centuries.
beats.source_passage: the best artisans and artists of the kingdom and thus realize the artistic mission Henri IV had set for the Louvre

beats.script_body: Louis XIV was just 14 when he settled in the Louvre in 1652, after the princely rebellion of la Fronde had been quelled. He never liked the palace, but while there he channelled enormous energy into it — scintillating balls, ceremonial dinners of twenty courses, performances of plays by Corneille and Moliere. His Majesty and his brother Monsieur were great lovers of theatre, unlike their grandfather Henri IV, who once confided to a woman friend: 'Yesterday evening I saw the comedians play, when I fell asleep. It was midnight when they finished.' During Louis XIV's reign, the Louvre's painting collection grew from 200 to 2,000 works, driven by the feverish acquisitions of his minister Mazarin and Mazarin's successor Colbert, supported by donations from Nicolas Fouquet, the king's wealthy treasurer, before his disgrace.
beats.source_passage: During the reign of Louis XIV the number of paintings in the Louvre increased from 200 to 2,000

beats.script_body: When Louis XIV moved his court to Versailles in 1682, the Louvre descended into a bizarre state of decay. The King's own apartment, left vacant, was taken over by the Academie des Sciences, which filled it with an elephant skeleton, a stuffed camel, and various anatomical organs floating in alcohol-filled jars. Booths and stalls crammed the courtyard. The panelling of the royal apartments was torn off, and painted ceilings were drilled through to make room for skylights and stove pipes. A motley population of artisans, parasitical courtiers, and prowlers replaced the splendid court. The five newly founded Academies, paradoxically, contributed to the deterioration of the very palace they occupied.
beats.source_passage: The King's apartment became the premises of the Academie des Sciences, housing an elephant skeleton, a stuffed camel and various anatomical organs floating in alcohol-filled jars

beats.script_body: Louis XIV's decision to move the court to Versailles in 1682 was not about architecture — it was about control. The Parisian aristocracy had grown dangerously independent, enjoying intellectual stimulation in the literary salons of enlightened ladies on the Faubourg Saint-Honore and Faubourg Saint-Germain. Louis had not forgotten the princely rebellion of the Fronde in 1650, which forced him into exile at Saint-Germain-en-Laye and ended his idyllic childhood at the Palais-Royal, where little Marie, his mother's chambermaid's daughter, had played his queen. By transferring the aristocracy to what the author calls a 'glorified ghetto' at Versailles, the astute monarch asserted his divine right and reduced the proudest nobles of France to glamorous lackeys in his service.
beats.source_passage: It was precisely in order to keep a close eye on this increasingly independent aristocracy that the astute monarch transferred its members to the glorified ghetto of Versailles

beats.script_body: The painter Auguste Renoir grew up in one of the lanes that ran through the Esplanade of the Louvre, where royalty and the lower orders still lived side by side — an intimacy inconceivable today. Young Renoir was one of the little street urchins to whom Queen Amelie's ladies-in-waiting threw sweets through the window when the children made too much of a nuisance of themselves. His son, the celebrated film director Jean Renoir, later wondered 'how successive kings could have tolerated such a seedy neighbourhood under their very noses.'
beats.source_passage: The painter Auguste Renoir grew up in one of the lanes that then ran through the Esplanade of the Louvre

opening_hours_basis: Gated museum; hours from the Louvre's own published schedule, closed Tuesdays with late Friday opening.
visit_basis: The glass pyramid, the Cour Napoleon and the palace facades absorb half an hour outside; inside is the world's largest art museum with 35,000 works over several wings that would absorb a full day, capped at the 90-minute tour maximum plus a long security and ticket queue.
judgement_basis: The interior is a hushed gallery where quiet is expected and running is forbidden, and the courtyard has no significant free quiet seating away from crowds; the pyramid courtyard is lit, open and busy into the evening, so standing there after dark is fine.
queue_basis: Security into the glass pyramid, then ticket gates, produce a substantial line at midday; timed tickets shorten but do not remove it, and off-peak means opening or late afternoon.

anchors.label: The Pyramid courtyard
anchors.basis: Cour Napoleon is where a person stands back from the glass pyramid to take the palace's three wings in at once; the corpus's pyramid beats are told facing it. Half the footprint covers the courtyard between the wings.

anchors.label: The Carrousel du Louvre
anchors.basis: The underground mall runs beneath the courtyard; a person inside it stands under the inverted glass skylight where the corpus's fashion-show and entrance beats belong. Indoor: offered on the screen, the tap plays it — GPS decides nothing under the ground.

anchors.label: The Cour Carrée
anchors.basis: A person stands in the western half of the great square courtyard, the palace's four façades rising on every side; the Cour Carrée chapters are told looking at them from inside the square, not from the pyramid court beyond the Pavillon de l'Horloge.

name: Paris Catacombs
short_description: Underground ossuary in former quarry tunnels containing the carefully arranged remains of approximately six million people

beats.script_body: The Cimetiere des Saints-Innocents had been piling up the remains of generations of Parisians since Gallo-Roman days, at the corner of rue Berger and rue Saint-Denis. By the late 18th century, the stench of putrefaction and the danger of epidemics were so great that a general outcry arose. Voltaire considered it a barbarity that placed the French below the Hottentots. One journalist who opposed the demolition on religious grounds was sent to the Bastille prison for an entire year. The transfer to the newly opened catacombs began on 7 April 1786 and took 15 months. Night after night, eerie processions carried draped remains from the different cemeteries of Paris to their new abode, where six million of them now rest. Today, the Square des Innocents bustles with street performers around the Renaissance fountain, unaware they are treading the soil that once buried the innocent dead.
beats.source_passage: Night after night eerie processions carried draped remains from the different cemeteries of Paris to their new abode where six millions of them now rest

opening_hours_basis: Gated ticketed underground ossuary; hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Long underground tunnel route through the bone-lined ossuary of six million dead; the walk plus a notoriously long ticket queue would absorb over two hours, capped at the 90-minute tour maximum.
judgement_basis: A confined underground ossuary of narrow tunnels with no running room, no seating and no place to talk, and it is locked and inaccessible at night.
queue_basis: Occupancy underground is capped to a few hundred people at once, so entry moves at a trickle and the wall-standing wait can be twenty minutes or three hours with no reliable way to predict which, making any bound untrustworthy.

name: Pavillon de Flore
short_description: Southwest wing of the Louvre Palace that housed the Committee of Public Safety during the French Revolution

beats.script_body: The Pavillon de Flore was completed as part of Henri IV's Grande Galerie — the colossal 470-metre wing connecting the Louvre to the Palais des Tuileries along the Seine. The gallery met the Tuileries at right angles, with the elegant Pavillon de Flore marking the junction. The Pavillon de Marsan on the northern side of the Tuileries was added only later, at the time of Louis XIV.
beats.source_passage: It met the Palais des Tuileries at right angles and was completed by the elegant Pavillon de Flore

opening_hours_basis: A Louvre wing seen only from the outside on this walk_by_only stop, its facade stands in the open, not gated.
visit_basis: Ornate southwest wing of the Louvre Palace seen from the riverside and Tuileries; a facade you pause at briefly, no separate entrance for it.
judgement_basis: A Louvre palace wing passed by on foot along trafficked quays and passages with no free seating and nowhere enclosed for a child to run, but the central riverside location is lit and peopled at night.
queue_basis: This is a walk-by-only wing of the Louvre Palace viewed from the street or riverside with no separate entrance, so there is nothing to queue for.

name: Place Vendome
short_description: Octagonal 17th-century square with a 44-metre column cast from 1,200 captured cannons, ringed by luxury jewellers and the Ritz Paris

beats.script_body: French haute couture was born not on the grand boulevards of the 8th arrondissement where it lives today, but right here in the 1st — in the second half of the 19th century. The world of fashion concentrated around Place Vendome and the Tuileries to serve Empress Eugenie and the ladies of the Napoleonic nobility. Its illustrious forerunner was Charles Worth, the Empress's English couturier — a fitting irony that the most French of industries was pioneered by an Englishman. The legendary Ritz hotel opened on Place Vendome catering predominantly to affluent English visitors, who also frequented the fabulous jewellery shops on rue de Castiglione and rue de la Paix. For their convenience, WH Smith opened a Parisian branch at no. 248 rue de Rivoli. It would take another century for haute couture's centre of gravity to shift westward to the 8th arrondissement.
beats.source_passage: French haute couture was born in the ist arrondissement and the bordering 2nd in the second half of the 19th century

opening_hours_basis: Open octagonal public square with a column viewed freely from the pavement, not gated.
visit_basis: Octagonal 17th-century square with a tall bronze column at its centre ringed by uniform facades; you walk between vantage points around the column and along the arcades for about half an hour, with nothing to enter.
judgement_basis: An open octagonal square with vehicle traffic circulating and no free seating, offering no safe enclosed run-space, but it is central, well-lit and patrolled into the night.
queue_basis: An open public square walked into freely from surrounding streets with no gate or ticket, so there is no line.

name: Saint-Eustache
short_description: Second-largest church in Paris near Les Halles with the largest pipe organ in France and a Gothic-Renaissance hybrid style

beats.script_body: When the playwright Moliere died, the clergy of Saint-Eustache refused him a Christian burial. The church did not like 'stage men' and did not admit them into its fold — all the more so because those 'ill-mannered louts' would turn up in front of the church during Sunday morning mass to announce their forthcoming plays, entertainment more exciting than the sermon, thus inevitably turning many souls away from God. It took the direct intervention of the King himself to persuade the clergy to relent, and Moliere's funeral proceeded in riotous conditions. The funeral of the celebrated fable writer Jean de La Fontaine was also held at Saint-Eustache, apparently without the same drama.
beats.source_passage: it took the intervention of the King to persuade the clergy of Saint-Eustache to give this parishioner a Christian burial

beats.script_body: A plaque on the wall of the southern aisle records that the funeral service for Anna Maria Mozart was held at Saint-Eustache in July 1788. She had accompanied her son Wolfgang on his third and last visit to Paris — an unhappy visit that left him bereaved and embittered. No longer a Wunderkind, Mozart was ignored by a shallow, unmusical Parisian society and had to share with his mother an insalubrious, draughty flat at no. 10 rue du Gros-Chenet, today's rue du Sentier. She took ill in June and died wretchedly on 3 July. Mozart gave a heart-rending account of the event in his Correspondence. Resentful and contemptuous of Parisian society, he left the city the following September never to return.
physical_cues: A plaque on the wall of the southern aisle
beats.source_passage: A plaque on the wall of the southern aisle informs you that the funeral service for Anna Maria Mozart was held here in July 1788

beats.script_body: Because of its remarkable acoustics, Saint-Eustache became a venue for some of the most powerful musical performances in 19th-century Paris. In 1855, Berlioz attended a performance of his uplifting Te Deum here by 950 musicians. In 1886, Liszt's majestic Grand Mass was premiered in the church, also in the presence of its composer. The famous choir was directed by none other than Charles Gounod, composer of Faust. Gounod's most outstanding pupil was a child by the name of Auguste Renoir — who felt a deeper urge to use his hands as a painter rather than as a singer, and went on to become one of the great Impressionists.
beats.source_passage: In 1855 Berlioz attended a performance of his uplifting Te Deum by 950 musicians

beats.script_body: Saint-Eustache houses one of the most fabulous organs in Paris, built by the Dutch establishment Peter Jan Van Den Heuvel and installed in 1989. Its beautiful case was designed in the 19th century by Victor Baltard — the same architect who designed the iron pavilions of the Les Halles market next door. Equipped with both a mechanical and an electronic transmission system, it is the largest organ in France, making it particularly well suited for performances of 20th-century music.
physical_cues: as you make your way out through the northern aisle, you will notice in the wall a colourful niche depicting the life of the central market of Les Halles
beats.source_passage: the work of the Dutch establishment Peter Jan Van Den Heuvel. It was installed in 1989

beats.script_body: Saint-Eustache served as the parish church to some of the most powerful figures in French history. Louis XIII received his first holy communion within its walls. Madame de Pompadour, the famous mistress of Louis XV, was baptised here. The composer Lully was married at Saint-Eustache, and Rameau — another of France's great composers — was buried here. The church's association with both Richelieu and the congregation of the plebeian Les Halles market next door captures the 1st arrondissement's signature contrast between high and low.
beats.source_passage: Richelieu and the names of the greats are also associated with this church, where Louis XIII received his first holy communion

opening_hours_basis: Gated church you enter; transcribed from OSM tag 'Mo-Fr 09:30-19:00; Sa 10:00-19:00; Su 09:00-19:00'.
visit_basis: Second-largest church in Paris, a Gothic-Renaissance hybrid with the country's largest organ and soaring vaults; interior takes about 25 min, exterior facing Les Halles a few minutes.
judgement_basis: The church itself is a quiet interior forbidding running, but it fronts the traffic-free Les Halles gardens with benches and lawns where two people can sit and talk, and the surrounding pedestrian district stays lit and busy after dark.
queue_basis: A large free-entry church near Les Halles with open doors and no ticket or security check, so entry is immediate and no line forms.
